toxins.name: Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (jacobine, seneciphylline, retrorsine)
toxins.chemical_formula: Not provided in the given sources.
toxins.description: in cats: The pyrrolizidine alkaloids of Ragwort (Senecio jacobaea) are metabolised in the liver to reactive pyrroles that crosslink DNA and destroy hepatocytes, causing cumulative, often irreversible liver damage
toxins.concentration_notes: The plant must be ingested in large quantities to cause liver damage. Fortunately, the plant is quite unpleasant to eat, which naturally deters most cats from consuming enough to be harmed

toxins.name: Thujone and sesquiterpene lactones
toxins.chemical_formula: Not provided in the given sources.
toxins.description: in cats: Common Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) contains the volatile-oil compound thujone together with sesquiterpene lactones; these are the toxic principles of Tansy and are distinct from the pyrrolizidine alkaloids of Ragwort
toxins.concentration_notes: It is toxic when ingested in large quantities, but the unpalatable nature of the plant typically prevents cats from eating dangerous amounts

symptoms.name: Liver damage
symptoms.onset: Not specified in the provided sources.
symptoms.notes: Liver damage occurs due to the pyrrolizidine alkaloid content of Ragwort. The cat must ingest the plant in large quantities to suffer this damage. Fortunately, Ragwort is quite unpleasant to eat, which usually acts as a natural deterrent and stops most cats from consuming it

treatments.name: Veterinary Consultation and Triage
treatments.description: Contact your veterinarian or a pet poison helpline immediately for professional advice2. If you have evidence of what the cat ate, take a sample of the plant (or a sample of the cat's vomit, especially if it contains plant matter) to the vet to aid in diagnosis
treatments.notes: You should not attempt to make the cat sick at home, as this may not be helpful and can cause further harm2. Fortunately, Ragwort is quite unpleasant to eat, which usually acts as a natural deterrent and stops most cats from consuming the large quantities necessary to cause severe liver damage. 2. Gastrointestinal Decontamination

treatments.name: Emesis Induction and Activated Charcoal
treatments.description: To prevent the plant's toxins from being fully absorbed into the bloodstream, a veterinarian may medically induce vomiting (emesis)3. This is typically followed by an antiemetic (anti-nausea medication) and doses of activated charcoal to bind to any remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract
treatments.notes: This decontamination step is most appropriate for a neurologically stable patient shortly after the plant has been ingested3. Due to enterohepatic recirculation (toxins cycling through the liver and intestines), multiple doses of activated charcoal may be recommended. 3. Liver Support and Protection

treatments.name: Hepatoprotective Therapy
treatments.description: Because Ragwort targets the liver1, the veterinary team will likely administer hepatoprotectants (liver-protecting medications) such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
treatments.notes: These specific medications are necessary to support liver function and aid in tissue repair if hepatic necrosis (liver cell death) is occurring or suspected. 4. Systemic Supportive Care and Monitoring

treatments.name: In-Hospital Monitoring and Symptomatic Support
treatments.description: The cat will likely require hospitalization for close monitoring, which includes evaluating liver enzymes daily for a period of time (e.g., 72 hours)3. The vet may also administer gastroprotectants to soothe the stomach and intestines
treatments.notes: If severe liver damage develops, secondary complications like hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) and bleeding disorders (coagulopathy) can occur4. The veterinary team will monitor blood glucose and coagulation profiles, and if hypoglycemia is present, they will administer a continuous intravenous infusion of dextrose
